posts.title: Kabuli Pulao with Beef Roast: A Satisfying Home Cook Success
posts.content:
Due to the scarcity of lamb, I decided to put my own spin on Kabuli Pulao by substituting beef roast for the traditional lamb, and I'm thrilled with how it turned out. The beef proved remarkably tender—cooked low and slow, it practically melted in my mouth, rivaling what you'd expect from the classic preparation.

The rice was absolutely fluffy, each grain distinct and perfectly cooked. What really stood out was the beautiful balance of flavors: the mild spices provided a warm, understated backdrop that let the meat and rice shine without overwhelming the palate. The sweetness from the carrots and raisins cut through perfectly, adding a touch of brightness that elevated the dish beyond a simple one-note meal. That interplay between savory and sweet is what makes this dish so special.

This is genuinely filling, yet somehow also fulfilling in a way that makes you want to come back for seconds. It's exactly the kind of dish that says "care" without demanding hours in the kitchen.

Final verdict: 100% will make again. Whether you stick with lamb or venture into beef territory like I did, Kabuli Pulao deserves a regular spot in your cooking rotation.

posts.title: Tave Kosi: A Custard Revelation from the Balkans
posts.content:
Walking into this week's culinary adventure, I approached Tave Kosi with a healthy dose of skepticism. A yogurt-based custard? On meat? It sounded unconventional, but I'm glad I took the chance.

Once again, I made the substitution call—chuck roast instead of lamb—and it held up admirably. While I'll admit that lamb would likely have delivered a touch more tenderness, the beef proved to be a solid replacement that didn't shortchange the dish. What really won me over was the custard sauce itself. Despite my initial wariness, it was surprisingly good. There's a pleasant tartness to it that cuts through the richness of the meat, adding a brightness that keeps the dish from feeling heavy.

Allspice is the backbone of this dish's flavor profile, and it does the heavy lifting beautifully—warm, slightly sweet, with just enough complexity to make you wonder what you're tasting. It's the kind of flavor that lingers pleasantly after each bite.

This is one of those dishes that reminds you why regional cuisines exist: to solve the problem of how to make humble ingredients sing. Tave Kosi does exactly that.

Verdict: Definitely making this again. Lamb devotees might have an edge in tenderness, but don't sleep on the beef version—it's a worthy contender.

posts.title: Couscous Tfaya: A Moroccan Masterclass in Sweet and Savory Balance
posts.content:
This week I finally sourced proper lamb for Couscous Tfaya, and the difference was immediately apparent. After a two-hour braise, the meat achieved that holy grail of tenderness—nearly melting on the tongue with each bite. It was worth the wait and the hunt for quality lamb.

But the real star of this dish? The onions. Caramelized to golden perfection, they already possess a natural sweetness that's almost dessert-like. Then the recipe layers in golden raisins and honey, and suddenly you're experiencing something transcendent. That combination of caramelized onions, raisins, and honey creates a sauce that's neither quite sweet nor savory, but something beautifully in between—complex, luxurious, and utterly addictive.

Then there's the couscous itself. I'd never steamed couscous before this dish, and I'm genuinely converted. The difference between steamed and boiled is night and day—each grain remains distinct and fluffy, absorbing the flavors of the braise without becoming mushy or one-dimensional. It's a technique I'll never abandon now.

This is the kind of dish that makes you understand why these recipes have endured for generations. It's sophisticated without being fussy, and deeply satisfying.

Verdict: A revelation. The lamb, the technique, the flavor balance—everything clicked. This one's joining the regular rotation permanently.

posts.title: A Catalan Lesson in Scale and Broth
posts.content:
This week's journey took us to Andorra with Escudella i Carn d'Olla—a traditional Catalan stew that proved to be more humble than the standouts we've encountered on this culinary tour. It's not a bad dish by any measure, but it lands squarely in the middle of the pack when stacked against what's come before.

What this meal did teach me was respect for broth production. I started confidently with a Dutch oven, only to quickly realize I was in over my head. Cue the famous Jaws line: "We're gonna need a bigger pot." A hasty migration to the stock pot followed—a humbling reminder that some dishes demand more real estate than you anticipate. The upside? You learn something valuable every time you cook, even when the result isn't earth-shattering.

The standout component was the Pilota, the meatball-like addition that brought subtle warmth and depth. Cinnamon was the secret weapon here—present enough to make itself known without crossing into overpowering territory. It's a delicate balance, and it was executed well.

Escudella i Carn d'Olla is a dish born of tradition and practicality, not showmanship. Respectful, but not remarkable.

Verdict: Worth making once, but not rushing to make again. A solid entry on the tour, with valuable kitchen lessons in tow.

posts.title: Angolan Cuisine: Bold Promise, Muted Delivery
posts.content:
This week's culinary tour took us south of the equator to Angola, and I approached it with high expectations. The ingredient list alone suggested a fireworks show: peri peri peppers, cumin, garlic, onion, and red palm oil. On paper, this should have been a flavor bomb—the kind of dish that lingers on your palate and demands your attention.

Instead, I found myself disappointed. The dish fell short of the promise those bold ingredients suggested. The flavors felt muted, lacking the punch I anticipated. There's a particular challenge when working with unfamiliar cuisines—sometimes the execution just doesn't land, even when the components are sound.

The heat profile was curious: I breezed through the meal without much warmth, yet the in-laws were clearly feeling the burn. Peri peri is notoriously variable in intensity, and it seems mine packed more punch than anticipated for some at the table. That said, heat alone doesn't save a dish that's otherwise underwhelming.

This is one of those meals that serves as a reminder that not every culinary adventure ends in triumph. Sometimes you learn more from the misses than the hits.

Verdict: A pass. It was decent enough, but I won't be revisiting this one anytime soon. There are too many promising dishes waiting in the queue to circle back on this particular entry.

posts.title: Fungee and Pepperpot: Caribbean Comfort Done Right
posts.content:
What a name. Fungee and Pepperpot sounds like it could be a children's book, but what it actually delivers is a masterclass in Caribbean cooking. This dish immediately won me over with its wonderfully balanced flavors and the kind of rich, robust broth that makes you understand why certain recipes have survived centuries.

The foundation is solid: salt pork and ham hocks create a deep, savory backbone that anchors everything. Okra does double duty—thickening the broth while adding a subtle body that makes each spoonful feel substantial. Then comes the habanero, left whole for flavor infusion, adding just enough spice to create a pleasant tingle on the lips without crossing into uncomfortable territory. Even the mildest palates at the table were perfectly content, which speaks to the restraint and intelligence in the seasoning.

The Fungee itself is an interesting texture—it reminded me of an undercooked hush puppy, but in the best way possible. Rather than being a flaw, it adds character and a different mouthfeel that complements the broth. I've got leftovers, though, and I'm already planning an experiment: a little cheese mixed in, then fried to see if that transforms it into something even more interesting.

This is the kind of dish that settles into your bones—nourishing, flavorful, and deeply satisfying.

Verdict: Definitely adding to the rotation. Fungee and Pepperpot is exactly the kind of recipe worth revisiting again and again.

posts.title: Asado: The Perfect Marriage of Meat and Fire
posts.content:
This week's tour brought us to Argentina, and Asado delivered exactly what it promises: pure, unadulterated flavor born from the marriage of meat and fire. There's an elegance in that simplicity that doesn't require apology or embellishment.

We made the practical decision to forgo the optional meats—sourcing them around these parts proved more hassle than it was worth. No regrets. What remained was more than enough: quality meat cooked over live flame, its exterior charred and smoky, its interior perfectly rendered. That's the foundation, and it's a strong one.

Then comes chimichurri—that herbaceous, garlicky punch that elevates the meat without overwhelming it. Paired alongside a bright tomato and onion salad, you've got a meal that achieves perfect balance. The salad cuts through the richness of the meat, its acidity and freshness providing contrast without competing for attention.

Asado is the kind of dish that reminds you why some cuisines become legendary. There's no pretense here, no unnecessary fussiness. Just honest cooking, done well.

This is a meal I can absolutely get behind on a regular basis.

Verdict: A keeper. Asado earns a permanent spot in the rotation. Simple, satisfying, and unfailingly delicious.

posts.title: Armenia — Khorovats Grilled pork and vegetables served on lavash with fresh herbs
posts.content:
The Verdict: The pork came out juicy and tender, and the vegetables brought a nice smoky roastiness to the whole thing. The flavors were genuinely there — but the meal suffered hard from a lack of sauce. Laid out on lavash with fresh herbs it looked and smelled the part, but every bite felt dry without something to tie it all together. A tzatziki-style sauce would have been the perfect bridge. We'll make this again, but a sauce isn't optional next time — it's mandatory.

Rating: Flavors ✅ | Execution ⚠️ | Would Remake: Yes (with sauce)

posts.title: Australia — Meat Pie Shortcrust bottom, puff pastry top, savory beef filling, muffin tin individual portions + bonus 8-inch pie
posts.content:
The Verdict: It's meat. It's pie. It is exactly what it says it is, and there's something deeply satisfying about that. The two-day approach — filling made ahead so it's properly chilled before it goes in — paid off with clean layers and no soggy bottom. Shortcrust on the bottom did its structural job, puff pastry on top delivered the flake. Muffin tin sizing nailed the handheld individual-portion format that makes these iconic. The leftover filling and crust stretched naturally into a full 8-inch pie as well — a happy bonus that proves the recipe scales without any fuss. A squeeze of ketchup (as the Australians insist on calling it tomato sauce) and the whole thing clicked into place. Unpretentious, honest, and exactly right.

Rating: Execution ✅ | Authenticity ✅ | Would Remake: Yes — and probably often

posts.title: Austria — Wiener Schnitzel Beef tenderloin, breaded and pan-fried, traditional preparation
posts.content:
The Verdict: A meal that was already a household favorite before it even made the world cuisine rotation — so expectations were high and they were met. Veal is the traditional call, but even a shop that can source alligator and kangaroo drew the line there, so beef tenderloin stepped in and honestly held its own. The breading was the star — solid enough to hold its structure but light and fluffy in the bite, with real flavor rather than just being a coating. Clean, simple, satisfying in the way only a properly executed classic can be. This one doesn't need reinvention or a sauce debate. It just needs to be made again, and often.

Rating: Execution ✅ | Authenticity ✅ (spirit if not letter) | Would Remake: It's already a permanent fixture

posts.title: Azerbaijan — Plov Saffron basmati rice with lamb, cinnamon, dried fruits, water chestnuts, and gazmag crust
posts.content:
The Verdict: Back in the spice corridor where cinnamon and saffron do the heavy lifting, and it's good to be back. Azerbaijani Plov leans into the sweet-savory tension that defines so much of Middle Eastern cooking — dried apricots, prunes, and raisins nestled into fragrant saffron rice with lamb, with water chestnuts throwing in an unexpected textural contrast. The gazmag crust — the thin crispy layer that forms on the bottom of the pot — earned its legendary reputation immediately. Buttery, flavorful, and satisfying crunch that makes you understand why Azerbaijanis consider it the prize of the whole dish. The result was otherwise polarizing in the best way: Keli's father took one look at the dried fruits and declared it dessert for dinner, which honestly isn't the worst compliment a savory dish can receive. For those already comfortable in this flavor territory though, it hit every expected note and then some. Another Middle Eastern entry that simply didn't disappoint.

Rating: Flavor ✅ | Authenticity ✅ | Gazmag: Absolutely worth it | Crowd Reaction: Divided but memorable | Would Remake: Yes

posts.title: Bahamas — Cracked Conch  Breaded and fried conch with coleslaw and johnny cakes
posts.content: The Verdict: The flavors were genuinely there — cracked conch has a character all its own and that came through. The problem was textural. The muscle attachment area put up a fight that pounding alone couldn't fully resolve, leaving some bites unpleasantly chewy. Whether that's a technique issue or just the nature of the beast is hard to say, but it was enough to drag the experience down. The slaw ended up being the standout of the whole plate — which says something when it's supposed to be the side. Johnny cakes looked the part but came out dry, needing some moisture to deliver on the promise of their appearance. An interesting cultural entry that didn't quite land as a meal we'd want to revisit.

posts.title: Bahrain — Machboos  Spiced chicken and rice slow-cooked in aromatic broth, with dried black limes
posts.content:
The Verdict: A serious step up from last week's Bahamian struggles. Machboos is a dish where patience pays off, and the broth proved it — deeply layered with spice, it did double duty infusing both the rice and the chicken simultaneously so nothing on the plate was an afterthought. The dried black limes were the sleeper hit, bringing a sharp citrusy sourness that in any other context might feel aggressive, but here got beautifully mellowed and rounded out by the spice blend surrounding it. The chicken was fork tender, which at this level of broth saturation feels almost inevitable but is still deeply satisfying to achieve. Slivered almonds were forgotten at the store, but toasted cashews stepped in without missing a beat — a substitution that cost nothing in the final result. Another reminder that Middle Eastern and Gulf cooking rewards commitment to the process.

Rating: Flavor ✅ | Technique ✅ | Standout Element: The broth | Would Remake: Yes

posts.title: Bangladesh — Hilsa Curry
posts.content:
The Verdict: Walked in skeptical — the volume of mustard going into this dish raised some eyebrows — and walked out pleasantly surprised. The mustard presence is undeniably front and center, but rather than overwhelming, it settled into a bold and cohesive flavor profile that worked with the fish rather than against it. Pompano stood in admirably for the traditional Ilish, delivering lovely flaky and flavorful flesh that carried the curry well. The one recurring interruption was the bones — fish steaks being what they are, mindfulness at the table was required throughout. A solid dish, but the path forward is clear: fillets over steaks would remove the only real friction point and let the flavors do their job uninterrupted.

Rating: 3/5 | Would Remake: Yes — but with fillets | Substitution: Pompano for Ilish, no significant impact on flavor

posts.title: Barbados — Cou-Cou and Flying Fish Cornmeal and okra porridge with spiced tilapia in place of traditional flying fish
posts.content:
The Verdict: A callback to Week 6's Fungee from Antigua — the Caribbean cornmeal tradition showing up again in a different form, this time paired with fish rather than standing alone. A diplomatically good week for the in-laws to sit out: tilapia was beautifully filleted and bone-free, which would have satisfied the father-in-law's bone aversion, but the spice level would have sent the mother-in-law running regardless. Their loss. The flavors were absolutely there — the spiced fish carried the plate and the cou-cou grounded it in that familiar Caribbean starchy comfort. Not a weekly rotation dish, but one that earns a spot in the occasional repertoire without question.

Rating: Flavor ✅ | Would Remake: Occasionally | In-Law Compatibility: 0/2

posts.title: Belarus — Draniki Finely grated potato and onion pancakes with sour cream, mushroom gravy, and homemade peppered bacon
posts.content:
The Verdict: Potato pancakes have been a long-standing fixture in this kitchen, but always built on leftover mashed potatoes — so Draniki came in as a familiar concept with an unfamiliar technique. The difference that finely grated raw potato and onion makes is immediately apparent: the result is a wonderfully crisp exterior that lands somewhere between a potato pancake and a fried hashbrown, but with its own distinct identity. The skepticism about calling it a pancake over a crisp is understandable, but whatever you call it, the texture is the revelation. The accompaniments took it the rest of the way — sour cream, a rich mushroom gravy, and homemade peppered bacon transformed what could have been a humble side dish into a fully realized plate. Significant enough to retire the old mashed potato method entirely.

Rating: 4/5 | Would Remake: Yes — this is now the definitive potato pancake method | Standouts: Mushroom gravy and homemade peppered bacon

posts.title: Belgium — Moules-Frites Steamed mussels with twice-fried frites
posts.content:
The Verdict: A classic from the sea that fed all four of us — Keli, the in-laws, and myself. The 4.5 lbs of mussels came in with about half a pound dead on delivery, which is an acceptable ratio and left plenty to go around. The mussels themselves were a crowd pleaser across the board, with one notable exception: Keli was not charmed by the occasional bit of grit — "teeth rocks" as she calls them — which is a fair grievance and one that's hard to engineer around entirely with fresh mussels. The twice-fried frites were solid and the method was right, but could have gone a touch longer in the second fry for that extra crispiness — self-acknowledged and easily corrected next time. Worth noting that Hy-Vee came through as a reliable local source for seafood, which bodes well for future coastal dishes.

Rating: 3/5 | Would Remake: Yes | Notes: Source mussels carefully, push the second fry longer | In-Law Compatibility: High — minus Keli's grit encounter

posts.dish: Rice and Beans with Stew Chicken
posts.title: Belize — Stew Chicken with Rice and Beans and Fried Plantains Recado Rojo marinated chicken, coconut milk rice and beans, fried plantains
posts.content:
The Verdict: A perfect score and it earned every bit of it. Recado Rojo — the deep red achiote paste that anchors Belizean cooking — carries an aroma surprisingly reminiscent of cocktail sauce, which is an unexpected first impression for a marinade, but what it does to the chicken is anything but ordinary. Tender, juicy, and deeply flavored all the way through. The rice leaned creamy rather than distinct-grained, which in the presence of coconut milk is less a flaw and more a feature — the sweetness came through cleanly and tied the plate together. The fried plantains rounded it all out, adding that sweet caramelized contrast that the dish needed. A complete, balanced, and deeply satisfying plate from a cuisine that doesn't get nearly enough attention.

Rating: 5/5 | Would Remake: Regular rotation | Standout: Recado Rojo marinade | In-Law Compatibility: Didn't attend

posts.title: Benin — Amiwo (Akpan) Fermented corn flour porridge with beef chuck, shrimp powder, and habanero
posts.content:
The Verdict: A quiet week — just Keli and myself — and a half batch that turned out to be one of the better surprises of the project. Keli came in skeptical after reading the recipe, which is a fair reaction to fermented corn flour porridge with shrimp powder, and left genuinely impressed. Being able to source the actual fermented corn flour rather than having to approximate it made all the difference — the tangy fermented presence it brings is not something you can fake, and it tied the savory depth of the beef chuck and shrimp powder together in a way that felt cohesive and intentional rather than merely interesting. Half a habanero went in this round and delivered a noticeable but measured heat — good enough to confirm the direction, but next time a full one goes in. The method will feel familiar to anyone who has worked through the cornmeal dishes earlier in this project, but the fermented flour puts Amiwo in its own category. A dish that rewards authentic ingredients and exceeded expectations on both sides of the table.

Rating: 4/5 | Would Remake: Occasionally | Standout: Fermented corn flour — source the real thing | Heat: Half habanero — going full next time | Keli Verdict: Pleasantly surprised

posts.title: Bhutan — Ema Datshi Chili and cheese stew with Anaheim and Poblano peppers, feta and cream cheese blend, served over white rice
posts.content:
The Verdict: Going in with low expectations of a bland dish, and coming out with a split verdict that averaged to something worth making again. The pepper selection this week was dialed back for the in-laws — Anaheim and Poblano keeping things mild where Jalapeño and Serrano would have been the call for a Keli-and-Joseph-only evening. Keli and Lisa were enthusiastic enough to call it a 5, while a more critical eye put it closer to a 3 — the compromise landing at a fair 4. The real revelation was the feta, which carried the dish further than expected. The combination of feta and cream cheese worked, but the feta was clearly the heavy lifter — next time more of it goes in to push that tangy salty profile further forward. Peppers came out beautifully tender and the sauce played nicely over white rice. A dish that came in undersold and left with room to grow.

Rating: 4/5 | Would Remake: Yes | Standout: Feta — increase next time | Heat Level: In-law friendly this round | Keli & Lisa: 5/5 | Personal: 3/5

posts.title: Bolivia — Salteñas Baked beef pastry pockets with peas, served with homemade salsa
posts.content:
The Verdict: Salteñas are traditionally a morning or midday affair, but rules are suggestions and dinner worked just fine. Beef was the filling of choice this week out of respect for the father-in-law's chicken aversion, and despite a personal longstanding grudge against peas, authenticity won out — they stayed in. The verdict: barely noticeable and not worth the argument. A grudging peace has been made. The pastry was the highlight, coming out light, flaky, and structurally sound — holding everything together through handling without giving up. The one thing to chase next time is more broth inside; a properly juicy Salteña should release a little pool when cut open, and that element was missing. Homemade salsa as a dipping sauce was a smart call that everyone appreciated. A unanimous crowd pleaser that just needs a brothier filling and its proper place on a lunch table to hit its full potential.

Rating: 4/5 | Would Remake: Yes — brothier next time | Best Served: Lunch | Pastry: Spot on | Pea Aversion Overcome: Barely noticed | Crowd: Unanimous approval

posts.title: Bosnia and Herzegovina — Ćevapi Freshly ground beef brisket and lamb sausage with Ajvar, served in flatbread
posts.content:
The Verdict: A meal that landed differently depending on who you asked, which tells its own story. The father-in-law called it a 5, mother-in-law a 4.5, Keli a 4 — and personally it came in at a 3, with blandness being the sticking point. The Ćevapi itself is where the gap opened up. The technique was sound — brisket trimmed and freshly ground literally ten minutes before hitting the mixer, combined with lamb, spices, and sparkling water for a quick emulsion that chilled beautifully before cooking. The process was right, but the spice balance needs pushing further next time. Not heat necessarily — the Ajvar handles that dimension — but depth and seasoning in the meat itself. Speaking of Ajvar, it was unquestionably the most labor intensive component of the meal and worth every bit of it, though mild peppers this round kept it in-law friendly. The whole plate reads as a gyro cousin, which isn't a complaint, just context. A dish with clear potential that needs the seasoning dialed up to match the technique.

Rating: 3.5/5 averaged | Personal: 3 | Keli: 4 | Mother-in-law: 4.5 | Father-in-law: 5 | Would Remake: Yes — with bolder seasoning in the meat and hotter Ajvar when the in-laws sit out

posts.title: Botswana — Seswaa Slow-boiled oxtail, pounded and shredded, with pap and morogo
posts.content:
The Verdict: Botswana's national dish makes no apologies for its simplicity — no aromatics, no spice blend, no technique to hide behind. Just meat, salt, pepper, fire, and time. Oxtail was the cut of choice this week, and it rewarded the slow boil generously. The collagen breakdown made for a luxurious, almost silky broth that was worth sipping on its own, and the shredded meat itself came out with a melt-in-the-mouth quality that elemental cooking at its best produces. Nothing is covered up here — the salt and pepper exist only to let the meat speak for itself, and it had plenty to say. The pap was the unanimous crowd favorite — in-laws, Keli, and myself all in agreement, which at this table is a notable achievement. The morogo was the one misstep, and purely a volume call — spinach wilts down dramatically and next time the amount gets doubled without question. Keli would have called it a 5 but the fat content held her back, keeping the table at a rare unanimous score.

Rating: 4/5 across the board — Joseph, Keli, Inlaws | Would Remake: Yes | Standout: Pap — unanimous favorite | Note: Double the morogo next time | Keli footnote: Would be a 5 with less fat

posts.title: Brazil — Feijoada  Rating: 3.5/5 (Joseph) · 5/5 (Keli, Lisa, Kevin) — Remake: Yes
posts.content:
Went with a Missouri-adapted feijoada since several traditional cuts weren't available. Substitutions: smoked pork knuckle, Spanish chorizo, pork ribs, corned beef, and bacon in place of carne seca, smoked pork sausage, and salted pork; mustard greens standing in for collard greens (added a nice salty note). Served over basmati rice.

Cooked a day ahead and reheated — beans developed noticeably more flavor overnight. The real discovery was the farofa (butter, onion, toasted cassava flour, salt & pepper): underwhelming eaten on its own, but stirred into the beans at the end as a thickener it was a major flavor upgrade — went from "what's the point of this" to "why haven't I been doing this all along."

Unanimous hit with the in-laws and Keli; Joseph's 3.5 reflects the familiar "ham & beans, elevated," and the greens plus farofa are permanent keepers going forward — confirmed keeper.

posts.title: Brunei — Ambuyat
posts.content:
Ran into three ingredient gaps and adapted on the fly: tapioca starch in for unavailable sago starch, a homemade stand-in for tamarind paste, and shrimp powder (saved from an earlier week) in place of shrimp paste in both dipping sauces.

The main lesson was heat. Before the boiling water goes in, the starch-and-water mixture is a classic non-Newtonian fluid — not new territory for me, but a fun one for Keli to experience firsthand. Once I added the boiling water, though, it needed to carry a lot more heat than I expected to push the mixture from that white, pudding-like stage into the proper opaque, glue-like consistency ambuyat is supposed to have. I undershot it and needed Chef Mike's help finishing the transition. Once it got there, it did its job as a neutral carrier for the dipping sauces.

Sides were the stronger part of the plate: swai fillets air-fried with salt and turmeric were the standout, with spinach a close second. A couple of execution misses too — the eggs were boiled and cut, but forgotten until the middle of the meal, and the cucumber never got sliced.

Overall verdict: a memorable, worthwhile experiment in food texture, but not one I'll put in rotation.

Rating: 2/5 (Joseph) · 3/5 (Keli) — in-laws not present — Remake: No
